Screenshots read in full: all 4 fold shots (desktop-light, desktop-dark, mobile-light, mobile-dark -- clean hero, TOC, callouts, no FOUC/flash), all 10 desktop-light parts covering both figures and every code/output block, all 16 mobile-light parts top-to-bottom, and the mobile-dark parts covering both figures (parts 04, 11-12) plus the A* code/output block. No GFM tables are used anywhere in this article (all comparisons are OUTPUT-panel columns instead), which sidesteps the exact failure mode -- a table column vanishing off the right edge at 390px -- that was the BFS/DFS article's worst mobile bug.
justification: This is a clean, essentially pass-grade design round with no major issues. Both figures (the three-step relaxation walkthrough and the negative-edge counterexample) are genuinely explanatory rather than decorative, have correct <title>/<desc> pairs, use the site's d-box/d-box-accent/d-box-2/d-accent/d-bad color classes to remap cleanly between light and dark (verified by direct screenshot comparison at 390px in both themes), hold zero overflow, and their captions state the exact conclusion to draw (Figure 1: B finalizes at 2, not the direct edge's 10; Figure 2: the -5 edge is found one step too late because B is already closed). The article's central design risk -- printing algorithm traces as OUTPUT panels that could clip on a phone the way the BFS/DFS article's edge-count table did -- was avoided by deliberate column-width choices: the pop-trace table's columns are `pop`/`pri`/`note` (max ~24 chars per line), the path-reconstruction table's longest line is `F   6  A -> C -> B -> D -> F` (30 chars), and the A*-vs-Dijkstra comparison is `h=Manhattan     17        34` (29 chars) -- all comfortably inside the ~40-column mobile budget with room to spare, so nothing analogous to the BFS article's severed 'DFS edges' column exists here. The one predict-the-output exercise ('Predict what one heavier edge changes') was screenshotted end to end on mobile: the question shows no code or output, only the collapsed 'Show solution' toggle, and the trace/output live entirely inside :::solution:::, confirmed correct. The other two exercises ('Find what makes this Dijkstra slower, not wrong' and 'Measure what an exaggerated heuristic costs') are not predict-output exercises -- the first hands the reader a working, already-run program as the premise for an analysis question, and its own output is part of that premise, not a spoiler; the second's output is correctly confined to its solution block. All three collapse/expand correctly with no output leaking under the question in either case. Source citations are hyperlinked inline at the point of the claim throughout (e.g. the Dijkstra 1959 paper, Sedgewick & Wayne, the PriorityQueue docs, Hart/Nilsson/Raphael 1968) rather than only named in prose and left for the reader to match against a numbered list at the bottom -- an improvement over the pattern flagged in the BFS/DFS and binary-search design reviews. Against Sedgewick & Wayne's own site this article covers the same core algorithm plus a worked, runnable demonstration of exactly why .NET's PriorityQueue forces lazy deletion (which their site treats as an exercise for the reader, not a worked example) and a full A* extension with a real, non-toy maze. Against GeeksforGeeks' Dijkstra page, this article uses one consistent running graph across most examples instead of a new toy graph per section, and includes actual measured instrumentation (expanded-cell counts) rather than asserted complexity claims. The only findings worth logging are minor and non-blocking: a small, un-actioned performance headroom item and one missing but optional editorial artifact.
